title: Rahula the novice
hookLine: the boy sets out water for his father's feet, and the Buddha teaches him with the little water left in the vessel (MN 61)

cards: Rahula, the Buddha's son, is a novice now, a young monk in training, and tradition says he's about seven. He's staying at a place called Ambalatthika.

Toward evening he sees his father coming, and does what a good novice does: he sets out a seat, and water for washing the feet. The Buddha sits, washes his feet, and leaves a little water in the vessel.
That little water is the whole lesson plan. Rahula, he asks, do you see this little bit of water left over? Yes, sir.

teach.h: A LITTLE WATER LEFT IN THE VESSEL.
teach.b: First, the little left over. So little, the Buddha says, is the monk's life of one who isn't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie. It's a stark sentence for a child.
But look at what carries it: water Rahula fetched himself, minutes ago, with his own hands. Second, the vessel moves. The Buddha throws the water away.
Do you see? Yes, sir. Just so thrown away is the monk's life of one who lies without shame.
He turns the vessel upside down: just so overturned.
Then upright again, empty: do you see how empty and hollow it is? Just so empty. Picture after picture, all made with one small thing, each a question Rahula can answer.
The Buddha never asks Rahula to agree with an idea.
He asks him to look. Do you see? And the boy says yes each time, because he does see.
The teaching goes into his eyes before his memory. From here the same discourse moves on to an elephant and to a mirror, which we met last year.
But it starts with the ladle. Fourth, why a child is taught this way. Truthfulness can sound like a rule from above.
Here it's a vessel in a boy's hands: something full or empty, kept or thrown out, an image that could come back whenever he poured water.
Gentle, not because the words are soft, but because the lesson is something he can hold.

how: The teaching to Rahula at Ambalatthika (Majjhima Nikaya 61) is taught to novices and children in some Theravada communities as a first lesson in truthfulness and in reflecting before, during and after an action.

games.q: the ladle of water: tap the pairs.
p: so little is the life of one who lies

s: the Buddha gave Rahula a long lecture on lying
he asks a boy questions about water the boy fetched himself: do you see this?
the lesson starts with water Rahula set out for his father
Rahula prepared a seat and water for washing the feet; the Buddha left a little in the vessel.
this teaching is mainly about keeping things clean
the water is a picture: the vessel, kept, thrown out, overturned or empty, shows what a lie does to a monk's life.

games.q: you're the Buddha. your young son has just brought you water for your feet, and you want to teach him why lying matters. how do you begin?
o: tell him the rule and ask him to repeat it.
leave a little water and ask: do you see this?
games.why: he leaves a little water in the vessel and asks Rahula if he sees it, then throws it out, overturns the vessel and sets it upright, empty.

practice: Bring to mind a child you know, or the child you were, and one thing you'd like them to understand: kindness, honesty, patience.
Instead of the words, look for the ladle: what ordinary object in their day could carry it, a cup, a shoe, a bowl of cereal?
Turn it over in your mind, the way the Buddha turned the vessel; if no child comes to mind, do it for yourself.

wordCard.voice: Musavada, false speech. What the Buddha taught his son Rahula with the little water left in a vessel. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali musavada: false speech, lying. The subject of the ladle lesson.

carryVoice: Your line: the ladle of water. A lesson you can hold stays longer than a rule. That's day seven hundred fifty.
